title: Fitting a plasterboard window reveal lining
subtitle: Line the three faces of a masonry window reveal with plasterboard for a clean square finish
excerpt: How to cut and fix plasterboard to the head and two jambs of a masonry window reveal. Covers measuring and cutting, fixing to timber grounds, taping and jointing, and skimming the finished reveal.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK drylining trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The three surfaces of masonry exposed inside a window opening: the head (horizontal top surface), and the two jambs (vertical side surfaces). The reveal depth is the distance from the face of the external masonry to the window frame. In solid-walled houses the reveal can be 200 to 400 mm deep.

Lengths of 50 x 25 mm timber fixed to the masonry reveal faces to provide a nailing and screwing surface for plasterboard. Grounds are bedded in dabs of plaster or plugged and screwed to the masonry. They set the finished face level of the plasterboard.

content.text: with plasterboard gives a flat, smooth surface that can be skimmed or finished directly with jointing compound. The plasterboard is cut to fit the head and two jambs and fixed to
plugged and screwed to the masonry.

Cut three lengths of 50 x 25 mm timber: one for the head, one for each jamb. Drill and plug the masonry at 450 mm centres and screw the grounds flush with the window frame edge. Use a spirit level to check the jamb grounds are plumb and the head ground is level. If the masonry is out of plumb or level, pack behind the grounds with card or hardboard packers before tightening the screws.

Measure each reveal face separately; masonry reveals are rarely uniform in depth. Score the plasterboard face with a utility knife against a straight-edge, snap the board back over the score line, and cut through the paper backing. Fix the plasterboard to the timber grounds with 38 mm drywall screws at 150 mm centres, setting the screw heads just below the surface of the paper facing. Fit the head board first, then the two jamb boards. If the joint between jamb and head is tight, cut a small chamfer on the edge of the head board to allow a hairline gap for jointing compound.
Tape and joint the joints and corners

Apply a coat of jointing compound to the joint between the reveal plasterboard and the adjacent wall plasterboard using the filling knife. Press joint tape (paper tape or mesh tape) into the wet compound and smooth flat. Apply a second skim coat over the tape once the first has dried, feathering it at least 100 mm each side of the joint. At internal corners where the jamb meets the head, cut and fold the tape to the corner and bed it with compound. Fill screw dimples with compound in two passes.

Once the compound is fully dry, sand the joints and screw fills smooth with the sanding block. The reveal can now be skimmed with finish plaster in the same way as the adjacent wall, or painted directly with a mist coat of diluted emulsion followed by a full coat.

attrs.symptom: Gap between plasterboard and window frame
attrs.cause: The grounds were not fixed flush with the frame, or the board was cut short.
attrs.fix: Fill the gap with a bead of decorator's caulk, smooth with a damp finger, and paint over. Small gaps up to 5 mm are normal and expected.

attrs.symptom: Jointing compound cracks along the joint after painting
attrs.cause: Joint compound applied too thick in one pass, or the board moved slightly before the compound was fully dry.
attrs.fix: Rake out the cracked compound, re-tape with fresh compound, and allow to dry fully before painting.
